## What the default install gives you

The install command in the README, `bun install -g github:garrytan/gbrain#stable`, installs the current stable release. `git clone --branch stable` does the same. A new brain created by `gbrain init` (no earlier config file) is set to the stable channel, and an install with no channel set follows stable too. Every update path follows the channel in effect: the update notice, `gbrain check-update`, `gbrain upgrade`, `gbrain self-upgrade` and the opt-in automatic upgrades.

Check which channel you are on with `gbrain doctor`, which prints `channel=<channel>` when one is set.

## What stays the same on stable

Since 16 November 2026, stable comes with a written promise about what a script or an agent built on gbrain can rely on.

**What it covers:**

- Command names and their documented flags (the ones `gbrain <command> --help` and these docs describe).
- MCP tool names and their parameters.
- Documented config keys (`gbrain config set <key>`).
- The page file and frontmatter format.
- Exit codes and the top-level fields of `--json` output for documented commands.
- Upgrading a brain from any stable release of the last six months. The channel started on 28 October 2026, so today that means every stable release.

**How those things may change.** A removal or a rename is announced first, in a stable release: in the one-time upgrade notice and in the release notes. The old name or behaviour keeps working, with a warning that names the new one. It is removed no sooner than 14 days and two stable releases after that announcement. A change that makes a command or tool refuse something it used to accept counts as a break under this rule too.

**The one exception: security and data-loss fixes.** A fix for a security hole or for something that loses data may change behaviour at once. Its upgrade notice says which of the two it is and what you need to do. It may leave out how the problem worked until the fix has had time to reach people.

**What it does not cover:**

- Wording of messages meant for people (not `--json`), and undocumented or internal flags.
- The alpha channel. Its releases can change anything between one build and the next.
- Search ranking, speed and the exact results of model-backed features.
- Very large brains during an upgrade. The upgrade tests build small brains, on PGLite and on Postgres, with and without a git repository. The two-hour load test runs a 600,000-page brain on the new release but does not upgrade one. ## How often stable moves

The rule: an important fix reaches stable within a day once it has passed the full test suite and the load test in step 2; everything else rides a weekly move; and stable never sits more than seven days behind tested changes. The scheduled check can move it at most twice a day; a maintainer can also promote, or roll back, by hand. If nothing important is waiting, the 7-day rule is the next reason for stable to move, though it still waits for a release that passed the test in step 2. A fix for a problem only newer, non-stable releases have, or one that unblocks a single setup, waits for the weekly move; if you need it sooner, install that release by its tag (see "Pinning a version").

What that has meant so far: the first stable release was v0.60.474.0 on 28 October 2026. Between then and 15 November 2026 stable moved 9 more times: once on 6 November, 9.7 days later, and then on each of the 8 days from 8 to 15 November, because an important fix was waiting on each of those days. Each move carried every change released since the one before. Until then an important fix also included a fix for something that blocked people. From the release that carries this change on (decided 16 November 2026), only security, data-loss and stable-regression fixes move stable early, so expect it to move about once a week. To see the current pace, list every stable release:

```bash
git ls-remote --tags --refs https://github.com/garrytan/gbrain 'refs/tags/stable-v*'
```

## Staying on stable

Do nothing; it is the default. To set it explicitly, or to come back to it from the fast channel:

```bash
gbrain config set self_upgrade.channel stable
gbrain upgrade --dry-run --json   # what an upgrade would install, installing nothing
```

gbrain never downgrades you by itself. If you ran ahead on the fast channel and switch back, you stay on your release until stable passes it. The one exception is a release that was withdrawn (listed as `known_bad` in the stable record): an install on it is offered the current stable release, even when that is older.

Updates are not applied by themselves unless you opt in. The default `self_upgrade.mode` is `notify`: you are told an update exists and nothing is installed without your say-so.

## Pinning a version

Install an exact release tag with this command. Its first line checks that the tag exists. Its second line removes any gbrain Bun already has installed, because installing one tag over another can leave the old version running and damage Bun's global package list. Its third line installs the tag:

```bash
git ls-remote --exit-code --tags https://github.com/garrytan/gbrain refs/tags/v<version> >/dev/null && \
  { ! bun pm ls -g 2>/dev/null | grep -q 'gbrain@' || bun remove -g gbrain; } && \
  bun add -g --backend=copyfile github:garrytan/gbrain#v<version>
```

Replace `<version>` with a release number, for example `0.60.722.0`. The second line skips the removal when Bun has no gbrain installed, so the same command works on a machine that never had gbrain.

A tag-pinned install stays on that release through `bun update`. `gbrain upgrade` is what moves it, so don't run it while you want to stay put. To stop update checks and update notices as well:

```bash
gbrain config set self_upgrade.mode off
```

## Going back to an earlier release

Nothing is rolled back for you. To return to an earlier release, reinstall its tag:

```bash
git ls-remote --exit-code --tags https://github.com/garrytan/gbrain refs/tags/v<previous> >/dev/null && \
  { ! bun pm ls -g 2>/dev/null | grep -q 'gbrain@' || bun remove -g gbrain; } && \
  bun add -g --backend=copyfile github:garrytan/gbrain#v<previous>
```

The first line checks that the tag exists before anything is removed. If an upgrade fails to start, `gbrain upgrade` prints the steps for your install type. A bun-link (git clone) install goes back with `git -C <clone> checkout <previous sha> && bun install`.

Know one limit before you go back. Upgrades can move your database to a newer schema, and an older gbrain will then refuse to set up that schema, with the code `client_behind`. Reads and ordinary commands on the older gbrain still work. The fix is to upgrade that copy again.

## Where changes that need your attention are announced

- **The upgrade notice.** After an upgrade, the first command (or the first tool result an agent gets) shows a one-time `behavior_changes` notice. It lists each behaviour change in the releases you skipped over, in plain sentences, often naming the setting that turns it off. Read it again at any time with `gbrain doctor --only behavior_changes`.
- **The upgrade summary.** Once the new version is installed, `gbrain upgrade` prints a short summary of the behaviour changes since the version you had, before its migrations run: the ones that need you first, then changed defaults, then a count of fixes and additions. Changes from before each one was given a kind are counted as not classified yet.
- **The changelog.** [CHANGELOG.md](../CHANGELOG.md) has an entry for every release.
- **The GitHub release.** When stable moves, its GitHub release becomes "Latest" and its notes open with the same short summary of behaviour changes since the previous stable release, then list every changelog entry since it. While this rule is new, Latest can still point at a newer release that is not stable; that ends the first time stable passes it.

## What the fast builds are for

Every release is also published on the **alpha** channel, as a GitHub pre-release. Alpha is for people who want each fix the hour it lands, and its releases are the pool stable promotes from. Switch with `gbrain config set self_upgrade.channel alpha` (`latest` is accepted as another name for it), or try one upgrade without changing your setting with `gbrain upgrade --channel alpha`. The git tag that tracks alpha is called `latest-stable` for historical reasons. It is the alpha line, not the stable channel.

Choose native OAuth/PKCE or a private machine handoff for the intended harness. For login links, clients, permissions, or token lifecycle, follow [MCP administration](docs/mcp/ADMIN.md) or `skills/mcp-access/SKILL.md`. Ask gbrain before you `grep`, `cat`, `ls` or run SQL on the brain checkout: it reads the index across every source, ranks, filters and names the slug to read next. With the gbrain MCP server connected, call the tool of the same name instead of the CLI (one connection, no per-call startup). | Lookup | CLI | MCP tool | |---|---|---| | Find a page by name or path | `gbrain find [--type T] [--source S]` | `find_pages` | | Count pages by kind or source | `gbrain stats --by source,type [--since 30d] [--collapse-aliases]` | `get_stats` (needs an admin-scope token) | | Answer a question, search a topic | `gbrain query "" [--types '["meeting"]'] [--since 30d]` | `query` | | Pages with these words | `gbrain search "" [--match keyword] [--source S]` | `search` | | Read a known page | `gbrain get ` | `get_page` | | Read only the part a search hit points at | `gbrain get --around-chunk-id ` or `--lines '{"from":1,"count":200}'` | `get_page` | | What the brain knows about a person or company | `gbrain entity `, then `gbrain recall "" --json` | `entity`, `recall` | | Links, dated events, every page of a type | `gbrain backlinks `, `gbrain timeline `, `gbrain list --type T` | `get_backlinks`, `get_timeline`, `list_pages` | | Save a fact the user stated | `gbrain remember "" --entity --content-origin user_said --provenance ""` | `remember` | | Why a page didn't rank | `gbrain query "" --explain-target ` | `query` | | Which installed skill fits a request | `gbrain skills resolve --text "" --json` (after `gbrain skills index build`) | none (CLI only) | | Find something archived to B2, Supabase or S3 | `gbrain storage-find ""` | `storage_find` | Parse `--json` output instead of matching the text; notices go to stderr. Recall relevant saved context before answering. Resolve a person (an email sender, an attendee) only by an exact match (`gbrain whois `), never a search's top hit ([identity rule](skills/conventions/brain-first.md#identity-exact-match)). Save explicit requests to remember with provenance; confirm corrections against the stored record. Withdrawal (`forget`) removes a fact from active memory; history, source material, and private backups may remain. Never promise physical erasure. Verify changes with actual GBrain calls and distinguish a local test from a new-conversation test in the harness. Durable preferences and facts belong in shared memory when the user wants them recalled later. Transient task state, credentials, local configuration, and harness activation state do not. Typed edges rely on stdio's best-effort startup/idle sweeps, explicit host maintenance or authorized `add_link` calls. Configured model providers can receive text; Markdown export is not a full database backup. Read [memory boundaries](docs/guides/memory-boundaries.md) before promising portability, graph freshness, privacy, or recovery. ## Multi-agent rules for a shared brain checkout Several agents, crons and hooks often commit to one brain checkout on the same machine. In such a checkout: 1. **Commit and push with one command, naming your files:** `scripts/brain-commit-push.sh "" `, or `gbrain git commit-push -m "" -- ` when the brain has no helper. Never delete `.git/rebase-merge` before saving its autostash with `git stash store`. Outcomes, conflict recovery, a stuck rebase and the lock contract for host daemons: [docs/guides/shared-checkout-git.md](docs/guides/shared-checkout-git.md). ## Agent operator protocol Every gbrain error, refusal, degraded result and recommendation carries the same machine contract. The quick version: 1. Read `code` (fall back to `error` on older servers). `message` says what happened, `why` says why. 2. Follow `fix.next`: - `run` → run `fix.argv` (CLI) or call `fix.mcp` (MCP) exactly as given. - `ask_user` → relay `user_message` to the user and stop; run the fix only after they agree. - `tell_user_to_run` → give the user `fix.command`; it needs them or the brain host's operator. - `wait` → retry after the stated delay with the same request. - `report` → tell the user what happened and run `gbrain doctor --json`. 3. Then run `fix.verify` (always read-only) to confirm the fix worked. 4. Treat `[gbrain notice …]` blocks and `[AGENT]` blocks the same way. A degraded result is not proof of "no notes": a result stamped `[gbrain degraded: …]` (`_meta.degraded`, the CLI `degraded` key) is partial. Exit 3 always means "stop and ask the user". Exit 10 means the write was accepted and is still pending: never "not found" or "failed", so poll the receipt (`gbrain write-request `) before retrying, reporting or moving on. Full contract, transcripts, effects, exit codes and marker grammar: [`docs/protocol/AGENT_OPERATOR_v1.md`](./docs/protocol/AGENT_OPERATOR_v1.md). ## Read this order 1. `./AGENTS.md` (this file) — install + operating protocol. 2. [`./CLAUDE.md`](./CLAUDE.md) — orientation + resolver: architecture, cross-cutting invariants, the reference map, inline ship rules. It routes to on-demand detail docs: [`./docs/architecture/KEY_FILES.md`](./docs/architecture/KEY_FILES.md) (per-file index — read a file's entry before editing it), [`./docs/TESTING.md`](./docs/TESTING.md) (test tiers + isolation lint + E2E lifecycle), and [`./docs/architecture/thin-client.md`](./docs/architecture/thin-client.md) (remote-MCP seam). 3. [`./docs/architecture/brains-and-sources.md`](./docs/architecture/brains-and-sources.md) — the two-axis mental model (brain = which DB, source = which repo in the DB). Every query routes on both axes. Read before writing anything that touches brain ops. 4. [`./skills/conventions/brain-routing.md`](./skills/conventions/brain-routing.md) — agent-facing decision table: when to switch brain, when to switch source, how cross-brain federation works (latent-space only; the agent decides). 5. [`./skills/RESOLVER.md`](./skills/RESOLVER.md) — skill dispatcher. Read before any task. ## Trust boundary (critical) GBrain distinguishes **trusted local CLI callers** (`OperationContext.remote = false`, set by `src/cli.ts`) from **untrusted agent-facing callers** (`remote = true`, set by `src/mcp/server.ts`). Security-sensitive operations like `file_upload` tighten filesystem confinement when `remote = true` and default to strict behavior when unset. If you are writing or reviewing an operation, consult `src/core/operations.ts` for the contract. ## Common tasks - **Configure:** [`docs/ENGINES.md`](./docs/ENGINES.md), [`docs/guides/live-sync.md`](./docs/guides/live-sync.md), [`docs/mcp/DEPLOY.md`](./docs/mcp/DEPLOY.md), [`docs/guides/remote-mcp.md`](./docs/guides/remote-mcp.md) (`gbrain mcp expose`). - **Run gbrain from cron, workspace scripts and hooks:** every caller goes through one wrapper that sets `GBRAIN_HOME` (never `HOME`), loads the brain's env file and runs the installed binary, never `bun run src/cli.ts` with an inherited environment. Log stderr (never `2>/dev/null`: a `no_brain` refusal then reads as "no results"), check the exit code, keep hook output off stdout, allow at least 10 s per call, and never print the process environment into a transcript. On a managed brain, schedule `gbrain sources refresh `, and have scripts commit the files they write with `gbrain git commit-push -- `, never plain `git commit` (`gbrain doctor --only cron_gbrain_home` flags cron lines that skip the wrapper). Wrapper and rules: [cron-schedule.md](docs/guides/cron-schedule.md#calling-gbrain-unattended), [scripts and the managed checkout](docs/guides/shared-checkout-git.md#scripts-and-the-managed-checkout). - **Keep a page to some members of a shared source:** put `readable_by: [alice-example, group:team-a]` in its frontmatter (a whole folder: `gbrain access rule add --prefix / --readers --source `, preview then `--yes`; widening waits for `gbrain access apply`) and bind each member's credential (`gbrain access member add`, `gbrain auth rescope --token --member `); `gbrain access check --token ` and `--as ` preview what a member reads. Purge only on the user's explicit go for that purge ("scrub the repo" is not one), one page at a time, verifying each; a stopped batch stays stopped until the user says again ([data-loss gate](skills/data-loss-gate/SKILL.md)). - **Bring in your chat history:** `gbrain transcripts ingest` imports a downloaded ChatGPT / Claude export (or agent session logs); `gbrain connectors` connects the account and syncs new conversations live, incrementally and on an opt-in schedule (cookie/OAuth credentials stay on your machine, 0600). MCP op `find_trajectory` exposes the same data — read scope, visibility-filtered for remote callers. `gbrain think` uses this substrate automatically on temporal / knowledge_update intent (default ON; flip `think.trajectory_enabled=false` to opt out). Non-metric event rows (`meeting`, `job_change`, `location_change`) ride through the same pipeline via `facts.event_type`; pass `kind: 'event'` or `'all'` to `find_trajectory` to query them. - **Answer "who is waiting on me?":** connect the user's Google account once (`gbrain google setup` — two user interactions; relay the `[SHOW USER]` blocks verbatim), then `gbrain waiting --json` returns the ranked people waiting on the user, what they promised, evidence quotes, and Gmail deep links. Manage loops with `gbrain loops done|drop|mute`. It refuses on stale data and names the exact sync command to run first. Guide: [`docs/guides/system-one.md`](./docs/guides/system-one.md); key setup: [`docs/ai-providers/typesafe.md`](./docs/ai-providers/typesafe.md). - **Contribute code:** [`CONTRIBUTING.md`, "Where does my change go?"](./CONTRIBUTING.md#where-does-my-change-go) names the files, registry, regenerate command and smallest test for a storage method, schema migration, doctor check, CLI-only command, HTTP route or sync phase. A branch written before refactor wave 1: follow the moved-symbol map in [`docs/architecture/wave-1-porting.md`](./docs/architecture/wave-1-porting.md). - **Everything else:** [`./llms.txt`](./llms.txt) is the full documentation map. [`./llms-full.txt`](./llms-full.txt) is the same map with core docs inlined for single-fetch ingestion. ## Before shipping Easiest path: `bun run ci:local` runs the full CI gate inside Docker (gitleaks, guards + typecheck, then 4-shard parallel unit + E2E against four pgvector containers plus a transaction-mode PgBouncer; unit phase keeps `DATABASE_URL` unset) and tears down. `bun run ci:local:diff` checks a doc-only diff in seconds (gitleaks plus the doc checks) and runs the full gate otherwise. Requires Docker (Docker Desktop / OrbStack / Colima) and `gitleaks` (`brew install gitleaks`). Fastest path, with a Ubicloud token (`UBICLOUD_API_KEY` or `UBICLOUD_API_TOKEN`): `bun run ci:ubicloud` runs the same gate across four ephemeral VMs in about five minutes, uncommitted edits included (`ci:ubicloud:diff` for the doc-only fast path). Pass its test lanes the exact commands in [/ship lanes](docs/ci-event-parity.md#ship-lanes), so a passed full-ci run carries them. The full release + contributor process (CHANGELOG voice, version-locations sync, PR conventions, community-PR-wave) lives in [`./docs/RELEASING.md`](./docs/RELEASING.md); read it before shipping. **PRs carry no version** ([releases per batch](docs/RELEASING.md#releases-per-batch)): /ship writes a `changelog.d` fragment, and the release PR picks the next PATCH (never MINOR or MAJOR) and syncs every stamp. This changes numbering only: scope, merge, deployment, paid-work and validation approvals still apply. ## Privacy Never commit real names of people, companies, or funds into public artifacts. {"output": "# Connect GBrain to Hermes

> This page is the MCP-registration reference for Hermes (the NousResearch
> `hermes-agent`). For the full brain install — CLI, engine, skills, dream
> cycle — follow [INSTALL_FOR_AGENTS.md](../../INSTALL_FOR_AGENTS.md) first;
> this page wires the finished brain into Hermes over stdio MCP.

Hermes spawns `gbrain serve` as a local stdio subprocess. No server, no tunnel,
no token needed. Works with both PGLite and Supabase engines. No machine that
stays online? Hosted GBrain at [gbrain.io](https://gbrain.io/?ref=hermes-md) is always on.

## Register (recommended)

```bash
printf 'Y\n' | hermes mcp add gbrain --env GBRAIN_HOME=$HOME --connect-timeout 60 --command $(which gbrain) --args serve --surface starter --advertise verbs
```

The tool list shows the seven memory verbs (`recall`, `remember`, `entity`, …)
plus `request_tools`; every other operation stays callable, and `request_tools`
lists it and returns its schema. Drop `--advertise verbs` to list every
operation.

`hermes mcp add` performs a real MCP handshake and tool discovery at add time,
then prompts `Enable all N tools? [Y/n/select]:`. Three gotchas, all observed:

- **`--args` must be the LAST option.** Everything after it — including a
  misplaced `--env` — is swallowed into the server argv. To pass several
  environment variables, list them all after ONE `--env` flag
  (`--env A=1 B=2`); repeating the flag replaces the earlier values and the
  server is saved disabled when its handshake then fails. Put `--env` and
  `--connect-timeout` before `--command`, exactly as above.
- **Pipe the `Y` in non-interactive contexts.** EOF on the enable-tools prompt
  prints `Cancelled.` and saves nothing. The piped `Y` saves the server with
  all tools enabled.
- **The exit code is 0 even on connection failure or cancel.** Never assert on
  `mcp add`'s exit status — verify with `hermes mcp list` and
  `hermes mcp test gbrain` (below).

## Brain-first instructions

Registering the MCP server only makes the tools available. Agents seldom call a
brain nobody told them about, so finish the install with:

```bash
gbrain setup hermes --instructions-only
```

It writes one short marked block into `$HERMES_HOME/SOUL.md` (default `~/.hermes/SOUL.md`), after your identity
text, which stays first and unchanged: before answering any turn,
search the brain first, read the best hit, fill gaps with other tools, apply your own
access rules, then finish the task. Text outside the markers is never touched, a
re-run upgrades the block in place, `--dry-run` previews it,
`--no-instructions` opts out (and is remembered) and `--remove` takes it out.
`gbrain doctor` warns when the block is missing or out of date. Setup never
creates `SOUL.md`: Hermes uses a non-empty one instead of its default identity,
so start Hermes once (it seeds the file) or write your identity there first.

The same rule also rides every turn. Setup appends a marked `pre_llm_call` shell
hook to `$HERMES_HOME/config.yaml` and records its approval in Hermes's
